h1: Cleaning beer lines on a home kegerator
title: Cleaning Beer Lines on a Home Kegerator | Craft Beer School
desc: How often to clean home kegerator beer lines, the cleaner and method to use and how to strip down a tap so every pour tastes fresh.
teaser: Dirty beer lines make good homebrew taste bad. A 20 minute routine every few weeks keeps them clean.
standfirst: Beer lines collect yeast, sugar, proteins and beerstone every time beer runs through them. Left alone, that film breeds bacteria and taints every pour. Here is how often to clean a home kegerator, what to use and how to do it.
sections:
Every pour leaves a thin film inside the line and tap. Yeast, proteins, hop resins and sugars stick to the walls. Over weeks that film thickens and mineral deposits called beerstone build on top. Bacteria and wild yeast settle in. The first sign is often a buttery note from diacetyl made by bacteria such as Pediococcus. Sour or musty flavours follow. A dirty line can also make beer foam, because the rough surface gives carbon dioxide places to form bubbles.

The beer in the keg can be perfect while the glass tastes off. If one keg tastes fine through a clean line and stale through yours, the line is the problem.

Commercial bars are commonly advised to clean draught lines with an alkaline cleaner every two weeks and to use an acid cleaner every few months to remove beerstone. A home kegerator sees far less traffic, but the line sits full of beer at warmer temperatures for longer. A sensible home routine is:

  • Every keg change, or every two to four weeks if a keg lasts longer: alkaline clean, rinse and sanitise.
  • Every few months: an acid clean to remove beerstone, plus a full tap strip-down.
  • Every year or so: replace vinyl lines. They are cheap and slowly absorb flavours.

Use a proper draught line cleaner or an alkaline brewery cleaner. Line cleaners are usually caustic, based on sodium or potassium hydroxide. Brewery cleaners like percarbonate-based powders work well for home systems too. Follow the maker's dilution exactly. Many line cleaners work best warm, around 30 to 40 °C, so use warm water if the instructions say so.

Caustic cleaners burn skin and eyes. Wear gloves and eye protection, mix them in a well-ventilated space and keep them away from children. Never mix a caustic cleaner with an acid. Our guide to cleaning versus sanitising explains why the two are separate steps.

1. Disconnect the keg and the gas.
  2. Fill a spare keg, or a cleaning bottle with a keg coupler, with warm cleaner solution.
  3. Connect it to the beer line and gas. Push cleaner through until it runs from the tap.
  4. Leave it to soak for 15 to 20 minutes. Push a little more through halfway to refresh it.
  5. Rinse with clean water until no cleaner remains. Test the rinse with pH strips if your cleaner's instructions advise it.
  6. Push no-rinse sanitiser through the line and leave it for its contact time.
  7. Reconnect a keg and pour until the beer runs clear of sanitiser.

A small hand pump or a recirculating pump does a better job than a single push, because moving liquid scrubs the walls. A pump that keeps cleaner flowing for 15 minutes is ideal.

The tap is where residue builds fastest. Beer dries in the spout between pours. Every keg change, unscrew the tap from the shank, take it apart and soak the parts in cleaner. Scrub with a small brush and rinse. Check the seals and O-rings for wear. A worn seal lets air in, which dries beer inside the tap and attracts fruit flies in warm weather.

Forward-sealing taps keep beer behind the valve and dry less. Rear-sealing taps are more common on cheap kegerators and need more frequent cleaning. Rinse the spout with warm water after each session in either case.
Clean lines are part of quality

Draught quality is easy to overlook when the beer itself is good. In a hot Indian kitchen, though, residue in the lines grows bacteria faster than in a cool cellar. A neglected line can ruin a batch you spent weeks on. A clean system also pours with less foam, which makes balancing your kegerator easier.

Temperature matters too. The same steady cold that protects the beer in the keg also slows growth in the line. Our guide to temperature control at home covers the fridge controllers many brewers use for both jobs.

Your first step: buy a coupler cleaning bottle that fits your keg fittings and a small bottle of line cleaner. Put a date on the fridge door and clean the line when the current keg runs out.
faqs: How often should I clean home beer lines?
At every keg change or every two to four weeks, with an acid clean and full tap strip every few months.
Can I use dish soap to clean beer lines?
No. Soap leaves residues that kill beer foam and taint flavour. Use a draught line cleaner or an alkaline brewery cleaner.
Why does my beer taste buttery from the tap?
Diacetyl from bacteria growing in a dirty line is a common cause. Clean the line and tap, then taste again.
